misconceptions.trigger: Many early examples are one-dimensional, so learners overgeneralize scalar subtraction.
misconceptions.pattern: Relative motion can always be solved by subtracting speeds without considering direction.
misconceptions.description: Relative motion is a vector relationship. Direction and sign determine whether velocities add, subtract, or change heading.
misconceptions.feedback: If one object moves east and another moves north, can one signed number describe their full relative velocity?

misconceptions.trigger: Reference frames often feel like labels instead of physically meaningful choices.
misconceptions.pattern: A boat's speed through water is the same as its speed relative to the shore.
misconceptions.description: Those are different reference frames. Current or platform motion must be combined to get the ground-relative velocity.
misconceptions.feedback: What extra motion appears when the river itself is moving?

misconceptions.trigger: Everyday language tends to treat motion as absolute unless the frame is stated explicitly.
misconceptions.pattern: If one observer sees an object at rest, the object must be at rest for everyone.
misconceptions.description: Rest and motion are frame-dependent. An object can be stationary in one frame and moving quickly in another.
misconceptions.feedback: How can a passenger feel still on a train while a platform observer measures a large speed?
